items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "economics".
items.answer: The social science that studies how individuals, firms and governments allocate scarce resources among competing, unlimited wants
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the social science that studies how individuals, firms and governments allocate scarce resources among competing, unlimited wants. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a natural science such as physics and economics as a social science.
items.answer: Both use models and test hypotheses against evidence, but economics studies human behaviour, which changes and cannot be placed in controlled laboratory conditions, so results are less exact and depend on ceteris paribus.
items.markingKey: Both use models and test hypotheses against evidence, but economics studies human behaviour, which changes and cannot be placed in controlled laboratory conditions, so results are less exact and depend on ceteris paribus. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the ceteris paribus assumption is used when drawing a demand curve.
items.answer: A demand curve shows the relationship between price and quantity demanded only, holding income, tastes, prices of related goods and other determinants constant; if one of these changes the whole curve shifts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A demand curve shows the relationship between price and quantity demanded only, holding income, tastes, prices of related goods and other determinants constant; if one of these changes the whole curve shifts. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Ceteris paribus means that nothing in the economy ever changes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ceteris paribus is an analytical assumption that other variables are held constant only while the effect of one variable is studied; in reality many variables change together.
items.markingKey: Ceteris paribus is an analytical assumption that other variables are held constant only while the effect of one variable is studied; in reality many variables change together. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how an economist might test the hypothesis that a higher minimum wage reduces youth employment.
items.answer: Collect employment data for young workers before and after the change, compare with a similar region that did not change its minimum wage (a natural experiment), hold other factors constant as far as possible and accept, reject or refine the hypothesis.
items.markingKey: Collect employment data for young workers before and after the change, compare with a similar region that did not change its minimum wage (a natural experiment), hold other factors constant as far as possible and accept, reject or refine the hypothesis.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Economists predicted that a sugar tax would reduce consumption of sugary drinks. When the UK introduced its Soft Drinks Industry Levy in 2018, many manufacturers cut the sugar content of their drinks before the tax began, so the amount of sugar sold fell even though volumes of soft drinks sold did not fall by much.
— Extract based on reporting of the UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy

Using the extract, explain why the outcome of the policy was different from a simple model's prediction.
items.answer: The simple model assumes the product is unchanged and predicts lower quantity demanded as price rises; in reality firms responded by reformulating, so sales volumes held up while sugar intake fell – other variables (product characteristics) did not stay constant.
items.markingKey: The simple model assumes the product is unchanged and predicts lower quantity demanded as price rises; in reality firms responded by reformulating, so sales volumes held up while sugar intake fell – other variables (product characteristics) did not stay constant. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why economics is classed as a social science?
options: Its predictions are always exact
It uses mathematics and graphs
It is concerned only with money and prices
It studies human behaviour, which cannot usually be tested in controlled experiments
items.answer: It studies human behaviour, which cannot usually be tested in controlled experiments
items.markingKey: D. Economics studies people's choices; unlike the natural sciences, controlled experiments are rarely possible, so economists rely on models and ceteris paribus.

items.stem: A student claims that Ceteris paribus means that nothing in the economy ever changes. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ceteris paribus is an analytical assumption that other variables are held constant only while the effect of one variable is studied; in reality many variables change together.
items.markingKey: Ceteris paribus is an analytical assumption that other variables are held constant only while the effect of one variable is studied; in reality many variables change together. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Card and Krueger's 1994 study of fast-food employment in New Jersey and Pennsylvania and explain what it reveals about the use of natural experiments to test economic hypotheses.
items.answer: After New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992, employment in fast-food restaurants did not fall relative to neighbouring Pennsylvania. Economists cannot run controlled experiments, so they compare similar groups exposed to different policies; the result challenged the simple model's prediction and led to refined theories of labour markets.
items.markingKey: Context (After New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992, employment in fast-food restaurants did not fall relative to neighbouring Pennsylvania.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Economists cannot run controlled experiments, so they compare similar groups exposed to different policies; the result challenged the simple model's prediction and led to refined theories of labour markets. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of natural experiments to test economic hypotheses.

items.stem: Hana writes: "Economic models are useless because they are unrealistic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Models are deliberately simplified; their value lies in isolating key relationships and generating testable predictions. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by how realistic its assumptions are.
items.markingKey: Models are deliberately simplified; their value lies in isolating key relationships and generating testable predictions. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by how realistic its assumptions are. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that economics can never be as scientific as physics.
items.answer: Economics uses scientific methods but its subject matter makes results probabilistic rather than exact; it is a science of tendencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: human behaviour is less predictable than physical laws; controlled experiments are rarely possible; value judgements influence the questions economists ask. Arguments against: economists use the scientific method: hypotheses tested against data; randomised controlled trials and natural experiments are increasingly used (e.g. Nobel prize 2019 for field experiments); econometric methods allow some variables to be controlled statistically. Judgement: Economics uses scientific methods but its subject matter makes results probabilistic rather than exact; it is a science of tendencies. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Which of the following are the three basic economic questions?
options: What to export, what to import and what to save
What to buy, where to buy and when to buy
What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce
How much to tax, how much to spend and how much to borrow
items.answer: What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce
items.markingKey: C. Every society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, because resources are scarce.

items.stem: Explain the difference between wants and needs.
items.answer: Needs are the basic requirements for survival (food, shelter, clothing); wants are desires beyond needs and are unlimited, which is the root of scarcity.
items.markingKey: Needs are the basic requirements for survival (food, shelter, clothing); wants are desires beyond needs and are unlimited, which is the root of scarcity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Opportunity cost is the total of all the alternatives that are given up. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Opportunity cost is only the value of the single next best alternative forgone, not all the alternatives.
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost is only the value of the single next best alternative forgone, not all the alternatives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A government in Ghana has a budget of $50 million that it can spend on either a new hospital or 200 km of rural roads. It chooses the hospital. Identify the opportunity cost of this decision.
items.answer: The 200 km of rural roads that are given up (the next best alternative).
items.markingKey: The 200 km of rural roads that are given up (the next best alternative).

items.stem: Using the Covid-19 vaccine roll-out in 2021 as an example, explain scarcity and the 'for whom' question.
items.answer: Governments had limited doses and had to decide who would be vaccinated first, usually the elderly and health workers. Doses were scarce relative to demand, so a rationing rule had to decide who received them; giving a dose to one group meant another group waited.
items.markingKey: Context (Governments had limited doses and had to decide who would be vaccinated first, usually the elderly and health workers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Doses were scarce relative to demand, so a rationing rule had to decide who received them; giving a dose to one group meant another group waited. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to scarcity and the 'for whom' question.

items.stem: Explain how a country deciding whether to produce rice using tractors or using many farm workers is answering one of the basic economic questions.
items.answer: It is answering 'how to produce': choosing between a capital-intensive and a labour-intensive method, depending on the relative cost and availability of capital and labour.
items.markingKey: It is answering 'how to produce': choosing between a capital-intensive and a labour-intensive method, depending on the relative cost and availability of capital and labour.

items.stem: A city council in Lisbon can spend €20 million on either a new metro line extension or modernising 15 schools. Explain the concepts of scarcity, choice and opportunity cost using this example, and discuss one factor the council should consider in making its choice.
items.answer: Scarcity: limited budget versus many needs; choice: council must pick one; opportunity cost: whichever project is not chosen; factors: number of people who benefit, long-term returns (education human capital vs reduced congestion), equity, external benefits, opinion of voters.
items.markingKey: Scarcity: limited budget versus many needs; choice: council must pick one; opportunity cost: whichever project is not chosen; factors: number of people who benefit, long-term returns (education human capital vs reduced congestion), equity, external benefits, opinion of voters.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that free public services such as healthcare have no opportunity cost.
items.answer: Public services are free at the point of use but not free to society; they always involve an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: users pay nothing at the point of use; the service may be provided using otherwise idle resources. Arguments against: resources (doctors, hospitals) could be used elsewhere; taxes that fund them have alternative uses; waiting lists show the resources are scarce. Judgement: Public services are free at the point of use but not free to society; they always involve an opportunity cost. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. IB Paper 1(b)/2(d) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "economic good".
items.answer: A good that is scarce and therefore has an opportunity cost to produce or consume
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a good that is scarce and therefore has an opportunity cost to produce or consume. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why scarcity forces individuals and societies to make choices.
items.answer: Because resources are limited relative to unlimited wants, using resources for one purpose means they cannot be used for another; therefore every economic agent must choose, and each choice has an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Because resources are limited relative to unlimited wants, using resources for one purpose means they cannot be used for another; therefore every economic agent must choose, and each choice has an opportunity cost. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a free good and an economic good.
items.answer: An economic good is scarce, so producing or consuming it has an opportunity cost; a free good is so plentiful relative to wants that it has zero opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: An economic good is scarce, so producing or consuming it has an opportunity cost; a free good is so plentiful relative to wants that it has zero opportunity cost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the concept of opportunity cost arises from scarcity, using a production possibilities curve.
items.answer: Diagram: two goods (e.g. healthcare and education) on the axes; a concave PPC. Points on the curve are attainable and efficient; a point outside is unattainable because of scarcity. Moving along the curve from A to B gives more of one good only by giving up some of the other: that amount is the opportunity cost. Increasing opportunity cost explains the concave shape.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two goods (e.g. healthcare and education) on the axes; a concave PPC. Points on the curve are attainable and efficient; a point outside is unattainable because of scarcity. Moving along the curve from A to B gives more of one good only by giving up some of the other: that amount is the opportunity cost. Increasing opportunity cost explains the concave shape. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A university student in Toronto calculates that a year of full-time study costs CAD 8,000 in tuition and CAD 2,000 in books. By studying she also gives up a full-time job paying CAD 38,000 a year after tax.
— Hypothetical data

Using the information, calculate the opportunity cost of one year of study and explain your answer.
items.answer: Opportunity cost = forgone earnings CAD 38,000 plus the CAD 10,000 of tuition and books that could have been spent elsewhere = CAD 48,000 (living costs are excluded because they are paid whether she studies or works).
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = forgone earnings CAD 38,000 plus the CAD 10,000 of tuition and books that could have been spent elsewhere = CAD 48,000 (living costs are excluded because they are paid whether she studies or works). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.answer: Public services are free at the point of use but not free to society; they always involve an opportunity cost.

items.stem: Which key concept is most directly illustrated by a global semiconductor shortage halting car production in Europe?
items.answer: Interdependence
items.markingKey: Interdependence. Car makers depend on chip producers in Asia; a disruption in one part of the supply chain affects production elsewhere.

items.stem: Explain how the key concept of intervention links to market failure.
items.answer: When markets fail to allocate resources efficiently or equitably (e.g. externalities, public goods), governments may intervene with taxes, subsidies, regulation or provision to improve the outcome.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When markets fail to allocate resources efficiently or equitably (e.g. externalities, public goods), governments may intervene with taxes, subsidies, regulation or provision to improve the outcome. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why economic well-being cannot be measured by income alone.
items.answer: Well-being also depends on health, education, security, the environment and leisure; a country can have high income per capita but poor health outcomes or high inequality, so composite measures are needed. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Well-being also depends on health, education, security, the environment and leisure; a country can have high income per capita but poor health outcomes or high inequality, so composite measures are needed. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A government introduces free school meals for low-income families. Identify two key concepts that this policy illustrates.
items.answer: Equity (helping disadvantaged households) and intervention (government provision); economic well-being is also acceptable.
items.markingKey: Equity (helping disadvantaged households) and intervention (government provision); economic well-being is also acceptable.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Bhutan measures progress using a Gross National Happiness index, which includes psychological well-being, health, education, time use, cultural diversity, good governance, community vitality, ecological resilience and living standards.
— Based on the Centre for Bhutan Studies

Explain which key concept is illustrated by Bhutan's approach and why it differs from using GDP alone.
items.answer: Economic well-being: Bhutan includes non-income dimensions of quality of life; GDP measures only the value of output, so it ignores health, environment and how time is used.
items.markingKey: Economic well-being: Bhutan includes non-income dimensions of quality of life; GDP measures only the value of output, so it ignores health, environment and how time is used. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Efficiency should always be the main goal of economic policy."
items.answer: Efficiency is important, but policy must balance it against equity and sustainability; the right balance is a normative choice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficient use of resources maximises output and living standards; waste of scarce resources has an opportunity cost. Arguments against: efficient outcomes may be inequitable; short-run efficiency may undermine sustainability; well-being depends on more than output. Supported judgement: Efficiency is important, but policy must balance it against equity and sustainability; the right balance is a normative choice.

items.stem: Define the term "intervention".
items.answer: Government involvement in markets, through policies such as taxes, subsidies, regulation and provision, to change market outcomes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: government involvement in markets, through policies such as taxes, subsidies, regulation and provision, to change market outcomes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between efficiency and equity.
items.answer: Efficiency concerns making the best use of resources (maximising output or welfare); equity concerns the fairness of how that output is distributed. A market can be efficient but inequitable.
items.markingKey: Efficiency concerns making the best use of resources (maximising output or welfare); equity concerns the fairness of how that output is distributed. A market can be efficient but inequitable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Sustainability is only about the environment. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sustainability also includes social and economic aspects, such as sustainable public finances and maintaining human capital for future generations.
items.markingKey: Sustainability also includes social and economic aspects, such as sustainable public finances and maintaining human capital for future generations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Paris Agreement of 2015 as an example, explain the key concept of sustainability.
items.answer: Nearly 200 countries agreed to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. It recognises that current production and consumption threaten future generations, and sets targets to reduce emissions so that needs can be met over the long run.
items.markingKey: Context (Nearly 200 countries agreed to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It recognises that current production and consumption threaten future generations, and sets targets to reduce emissions so that needs can be met over the long run. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the key concept of sustainability.

items.stem: "Government intervention is the best way to achieve equity." Discuss.
items.answer: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets distribute according to purchasing power, not need; taxes and transfers can redistribute effectively; governments can provide merit goods to all. Arguments against: intervention can reduce incentives and efficiency; government failure: poorly targeted policies; NGOs, communities and firms (CSR) also improve equity. Supported judgement: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure. items.stem: Which economist argued in The General Theory (1936) that governments should increase spending to fight unemployment?
options: Karl Marx
John Maynard Keynes
Friedrich Hayek
Adam Smith
items.answer: John Maynard Keynes
items.markingKey: B. Keynes argued that insufficient aggregate demand could cause persistent unemployment and that government intervention was needed.

items.stem: Briefly explain why economists who agree on positive analysis may still disagree on policy.
items.answer: They may agree on the likely effects of a policy (positive) but place different values on the outcomes, such as efficiency versus equity, so their normative conclusions differ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They may agree on the likely effects of a policy (positive) but place different values on the outcomes, such as efficiency versus equity, so their normative conclusions differ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that a positive statement must be true. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A positive statement only needs to be testable; it can be shown to be false by evidence (e.g. 'raising tariffs increases employment').
items.markingKey: A positive statement only needs to be testable; it can be shown to be false by evidence (e.g. 'raising tariffs increases employment'). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the rise of behavioural economics, recognised by Nobel prizes to Daniel Kahneman (2002) and Richard Thaler (2017) as an example, explain the development of economic thought.
items.answer: Economists showed that people systematically deviate from rational choice, for example through loss aversion and present bias. Economic theory changes when evidence challenges its assumptions; behavioural findings led to new policy tools such as nudges.
items.markingKey: Context (Economists showed that people systematically deviate from rational choice, for example through loss aversion and present bias.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Economic theory changes when evidence challenges its assumptions; behavioural findings led to new policy tools such as nudges. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the development of economic thought.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Economists should restrict themselves to positive economics and leave normative questions to politicians.
items.answer: Economists should make clear when they move from positive to normative statements, but their analysis is valuable in normative debates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: positive analysis is testable and objective; economists have no special authority on values. Arguments against: policy choices always involve values; economists' expertise helps clarify trade-offs; choosing which questions to study is itself normative. Supported judgement: Economists should make clear when they move from positive to normative statements, but their analysis is valuable in normative debates.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Karl Marx was critical of the capitalist system.
items.answer: Marx argued that capitalists exploit workers by paying them less than the value they produce (surplus value), causing inequality, class conflict and recurring crises; he predicted capitalism would be replaced by socialism.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Marx argued that capitalists exploit workers by paying them less than the value they produce (surplus value), causing inequality, class conflict and recurring crises; he predicted capitalism would be replaced by socialism. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Adam Smith believed governments should play no role at all in the economy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Smith supported a limited role for the state, including defence, justice and some public works and education; he was not opposed to all government activity.
items.markingKey: Smith supported a limited role for the state, including defence, justice and some public works and education; he was not opposed to all government activity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify each statement as positive or normative: (i) 'Inflation in the euro area was above 8% in 2022.' (ii) 'The central bank should prioritise employment over low inflation.'
items.answer: (i) positive – it can be checked against data; (ii) normative – it is a value judgement about priorities.
items.markingKey: (i) positive – it can be checked against data; (ii) normative – it is a value judgement about priorities.

items.stem: "The ideas of Adam Smith are more relevant to modern economies than those of Keynes." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both remain relevant: Smith explains how markets coordinate activity, Keynes why governments must stabilise demand; modern mixed economies use both sets of ideas.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets and the price mechanism allocate most resources efficiently; division of labour and specialisation underpin global supply chains; competition drives innovation. Arguments against: the 2008 crisis and 2020 pandemic showed the need for active fiscal policy (Keynes); market failures require intervention; modern economies are mixed, drawing on both. Supported judgement: Both remain relevant: Smith explains how markets coordinate activity, Keynes why governments must stabilise demand; modern mixed economies use both sets of ideas. items.stem: Why does scarcity exist?
options: Resources are finite while wants are unlimited
Prices are too high
Governments restrict production
Some people are poor
items.answer: Resources are finite while wants are unlimited
items.markingKey: A. Scarcity is a universal condition facing all economies, rich and poor.

items.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of the social scientific method?
options: Collect data, publish results, then form a hypothesis
Assume ceteris paribus, then observe the result
Observe, form a hypothesis, test it against data, accept, reject or refine the theory
Form a theory, publish it, then collect data
items.answer: Observe, form a hypothesis, test it against data, accept, reject or refine the theory
items.markingKey: C. Economists move from observation to a testable hypothesis, test it with real-world data and revise the model.

items.stem: What lists contains only IB Economics key concepts?
items.answer: Scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, sustainability
items.markingKey: Scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, sustainability. The nine key concepts are scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention.

items.stem: Distinguish between Hayek's view of government and Keynes's view of government.
items.answer: Keynes saw an active role for government in managing demand to reduce unemployment; Hayek warned that intervention and planning distort price signals and threaten freedom, favouring free markets.
items.markingKey: Keynes saw an active role for government in managing demand to reduce unemployment; Hayek warned that intervention and planning distort price signals and threaten freedom, favouring free markets. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Scarcity only exists when there is a shortage of a product in the shops. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Scarcity is the permanent condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants; a shortage is a temporary situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price.
items.markingKey: Scarcity is the permanent condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants; a shortage is a temporary situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that economic models are useless because they are unrealistic. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Models are deliberately simplified; their value lies in isolating key relationships and generating testable predictions. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by how realistic its assumptions are.
items.markingKey: Models are deliberately simplified; their value lies in isolating key relationships and generating testable predictions. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by how realistic its assumptions are. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between efficiency and equity.
items.answer: Efficiency concerns making the best use of resources (maximising output or welfare); equity concerns the fairness of how that output is distributed. A market can be efficient but inequitable.
items.markingKey: Efficiency concerns making the best use of resources (maximising output or welfare); equity concerns the fairness of how that output is distributed. A market can be efficient but inequitable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between Hayek's view of government and Keynes's view of government.
items.answer: Keynes saw an active role for government in managing demand to reduce unemployment; Hayek warned that intervention and planning distort price signals and threaten freedom, favouring free markets.
items.markingKey: Keynes saw an active role for government in managing demand to reduce unemployment; Hayek warned that intervention and planning distort price signals and threaten freedom, favouring free markets. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sana writes: "Something that is free to consumers, such as state school education, is a free good." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: State education is free at the point of use but uses scarce resources (teachers, buildings) paid for through taxes, so it has an opportunity cost; it is an economic good, not a free good.
items.markingKey: State education is free at the point of use but uses scarce resources (teachers, buildings) paid for through taxes, so it has an opportunity cost; it is an economic good, not a free good. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Finland's basic income experiment (2017-2018) as an example, explain how economists test hypotheses with real-world data.
items.answer: 2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month unconditionally and their outcomes were compared with a control group. A randomised trial let researchers isolate the effect of an unconditional payment on employment and well-being, holding other factors constant by comparison with the control group.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "An equitable distribution of income means everyone earns exactly the same." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That describes equality. Equity is about fairness, which is a normative idea; many people regard some differences in income (e.g. for effort or skill) as fair.
items.markingKey: That describes equality. Equity is about fairness, which is a normative idea; many people regard some differences in income (e.g. for effort or skill) as fair. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a positive analysis of a tax can inform, but not settle, a normative debate about whether it should be introduced.
items.answer: Diagram: supply and demand for a good with a specific tax shifting S to S+tax; price rises, quantity falls, tax revenue and welfare loss shown. These effects are positive (testable). Whether the tax should be introduced depends on value judgements, e.g. weighing revenue and reduced consumption of a harmful good against higher prices for low-income consumers.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Germany's decision in 2022 to create a €100 billion fund for its armed forces shows opportunity cost for governments.
items.answer: After the invasion of Ukraine, the German government committed €100 billion to defence modernisation. The funds could have been used for other priorities such as climate investment or education, which is the opportunity cost of higher defence spending.
items.markingKey: Context (After the invasion of Ukraine, the German government committed €100 billion to defence modernisation.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The funds could have been used for other priorities such as climate investment or education, which is the opportunity cost of higher defence spending. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to opportunity cost for governments.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a demand curve is drawn on the assumption of ceteris paribus, and what happens to the curve when one of the other factors changes.
items.answer: Diagram: price on the vertical axis, quantity demanded on the horizontal axis; downward-sloping D1. With other factors constant a price change causes a movement along D1. If income (a non-price determinant) rises for a normal good, ceteris paribus no longer holds and the curve shifts right to D2; at every price more is demanded.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Paris Agreement of 2015 shows the key concept of sustainability.
items.answer: Nearly 200 countries agreed to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. It recognises that current production and consumption threaten future generations, and sets targets to reduce emissions so that needs can be met over the long run.
items.markingKey: Context (Nearly 200 countries agreed to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It recognises that current production and consumption threaten future generations, and sets targets to reduce emissions so that needs can be met over the long run. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the key concept of sustainability.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the rise of behavioural economics, recognised by Nobel prizes to Daniel Kahneman (2002) and Richard Thaler (2017) shows the development of economic thought.
items.answer: Economists showed that people systematically deviate from rational choice, for example through loss aversion and present bias. Economic theory changes when evidence challenges its assumptions; behavioural findings led to new policy tools such as nudges.
items.markingKey: Context (Economists showed that people systematically deviate from rational choice, for example through loss aversion and present bias.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Economic theory changes when evidence challenges its assumptions; behavioural findings led to new policy tools such as nudges. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the development of economic thought.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Scarcity will eventually disappear as technology improves.
items.answer: Technology can ease scarcity of particular goods but scarcity as a condition remains because wants are unlimited.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: technology increases productivity and potential output; some goods (digital files) can be copied at near-zero cost. Arguments against: wants grow as incomes rise; natural resources and time remain finite; environmental limits create new scarcities. Supported judgement: Technology can ease scarcity of particular goods but scarcity as a condition remains because wants are unlimited.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that the use of ceteris paribus makes economic models of little value for real-world policy decisions.
items.answer: Ceteris paribus limits precision but is essential for analysis; models remain valuable if their assumptions are understood and predictions are tested against evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real markets never hold other variables constant; policy makers need predictions that hold when many variables change together; unrealistic assumptions can lead to policy mistakes. Arguments against: isolating one relationship is the only way to understand cause and effect; models can be extended to include more variables and tested with data; models such as supply and demand predict the direction of change well. Judgement: Ceteris paribus limits precision but is essential for analysis; models remain valuable if their assumptions are understood and predictions are tested against evidence. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using one real-world example, explain how two of the nine key concepts can be in conflict.
items.answer: e.g. coal mining in Australia or Indonesia: efficiency/economic well-being (jobs, export earnings, cheap energy) versus sustainability (emissions, environmental damage); or efficiency vs equity in a minimum wage. Explain each concept, show the trade-off and comment on how policy might balance them.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that the ideas of Adam Smith are more relevant to modern economies than those of Keynes.
items.answer: Both remain relevant: Smith explains how markets coordinate activity, Keynes why governments must stabilise demand; modern mixed economies use both sets of ideas.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets and the price mechanism allocate most resources efficiently; division of labour and specialisation underpin global supply chains; competition drives innovation. Arguments against: the 2008 crisis and 2020 pandemic showed the need for active fiscal policy (Keynes); market failures require intervention; modern economies are mixed, drawing on both. Judgement: Both remain relevant: Smith explains how markets coordinate activity, Keynes why governments must stabilise demand; modern mixed economies use both sets of ideas. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "economic good"?
options: Statements about what ought to be, based on value judgements, which cannot be tested
A good that is scarce and therefore has an opportunity cost to produce or consume
A testable statement about the relationship between economic variables, derived from a theory or model
Making the best use of scarce resources so that waste is minimised; allocative efficiency occurs when resources produce the mix of goods society values most
items.answer: A good that is scarce and therefore has an opportunity cost to produce or consume
items.markingKey: B. "economic good" is a good that is scarce and therefore has an opportunity cost to produce or consume.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hypothesis"?
options: Goods and services essential for survival, such as food, water and shelter
Statements about what ought to be, based on value judgements, which cannot be tested
A testable statement about the relationship between economic variables, derived from a theory or model
The way economic agents, sectors and countries rely on each other, so a change in one affects others
items.answer: A testable statement about the relationship between economic variables, derived from a theory or model
items.markingKey: C. "hypothesis" is a testable statement about the relationship between economic variables, derived from a theory or model.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "intervention".
items.answer: Government involvement in markets, through policies such as taxes, subsidies, regulation and provision, to change market outcomes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: government involvement in markets, through policies such as taxes, subsidies, regulation and provision, to change market outcomes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the statement 'the government should ban single-use plastics' is normative.
items.answer: It expresses a value judgement about what ought to be done and cannot be proven true or false by evidence; it depends on how one weighs environmental benefits against costs to firms and consumers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It expresses a value judgement about what ought to be done and cannot be proven true or false by evidence; it depends on how one weighs environmental benefits against costs to firms and consumers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why opportunity cost is not the same as the money price of a good.
items.answer: The money price is what is paid; opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which can include time and other uses of the money. Two people paying the same price may face different opportunity costs.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The money price is what is paid; opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which can include time and other uses of the money. Two people paying the same price may face different opportunity costs. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between economics as a social science and a natural science such as physics.
items.answer: Both use models and test hypotheses against evidence, but economics studies human behaviour, which changes and cannot be placed in controlled laboratory conditions, so results are less exact and depend on ceteris paribus.
items.markingKey: Both use models and test hypotheses against evidence, but economics studies human behaviour, which changes and cannot be placed in controlled laboratory conditions, so results are less exact and depend on ceteris paribus. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "An equitable distribution of income means everyone earns exactly the same." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That describes equality. Equity is about fairness, which is a normative idea; many people regard some differences in income (e.g. for effort or skill) as fair.
items.markingKey: That describes equality. Equity is about fairness, which is a normative idea; many people regard some differences in income (e.g. for effort or skill) as fair. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "A positive statement must be true." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A positive statement only needs to be testable; it can be shown to be false by evidence (e.g. 'raising tariffs increases employment').
items.markingKey: A positive statement only needs to be testable; it can be shown to be false by evidence (e.g. 'raising tariffs increases employment'). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that Something that is free to consumers, such as state school education, is a free good. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: State education is free at the point of use but uses scarce resources (teachers, buildings) paid for through taxes, so it has an opportunity cost; it is an economic good, not a free good.
items.markingKey: State education is free at the point of use but uses scarce resources (teachers, buildings) paid for through taxes, so it has an opportunity cost; it is an economic good, not a free good. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A researcher wants to know whether a rise in bus fares in Nairobi reduces the number of journeys. Identify one variable she must hold constant (ceteris paribus) and explain why.
items.answer: For example the price of matatu (minibus) fares, household income or fuel prices; if these changed at the same time, the fall in journeys could not be attributed to the fare rise alone.
items.markingKey: For example the price of matatu (minibus) fares, household income or fuel prices; if these changed at the same time, the fall in journeys could not be attributed to the fare rise alone.

items.stem: A student claims that Adam Smith believed governments should play no role at all in the economy. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Smith supported a limited role for the state, including defence, justice and some public works and education; he was not opposed to all government activity.
items.markingKey: Smith supported a limited role for the state, including defence, justice and some public works and education; he was not opposed to all government activity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Noah could work 6 hours at a café in Mumbai for $15 an hour. Instead Noah goes to a music festival: the ticket costs $40 and travel costs $5. Calculate the full opportunity cost of attending and explain why the money cost alone understates it.
items.markingKey: Explicit costs $40 + $5 = $45; forgone earnings 6 × $15 = $90; total = $135. [1] explicit costs, [1] forgone wages, [1] total, [1] explanation: the money price ignores the next best use of time.

items.stem: Using the 2021 Suez Canal blockage by the container ship Ever Given as an example, explain the key concept of interdependence.
items.answer: A single ship blocked the canal for six days, delaying an estimated $9-10 billion of trade per day. Global supply chains depend on key routes; a disruption in one place delayed goods and raised costs for firms and consumers around the world.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The concept of opportunity cost is the most important idea in economics."
items.answer: Opportunity cost is fundamental because it follows directly from scarcity, but it must be used alongside other concepts and is often difficult to quantify.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every choice under scarcity has an opportunity cost; it applies to individuals, firms and governments; it underlies the PPC, comparative advantage and cost-benefit analysis. Arguments against: opportunity costs are hard to measure in money terms; people may not consider opportunity costs (bounded rationality); other concepts such as equity or sustainability also matter. Supported judgement: Opportunity cost is fundamental because it follows directly from scarcity, but it must be used alongside other concepts and is often difficult to quantify.

items.stem: "Economics can never be as scientific as physics." Discuss.
items.answer: Economics uses scientific methods but its subject matter makes results probabilistic rather than exact; it is a science of tendencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: human behaviour is less predictable than physical laws; controlled experiments are rarely possible; value judgements influence the questions economists ask. Arguments against: economists use the scientific method: hypotheses tested against data; randomised controlled trials and natural experiments are increasingly used (e.g. Nobel prize 2019 for field experiments); econometric methods allow some variables to be controlled statistically. Supported judgement: Economics uses scientific methods but its subject matter makes results probabilistic rather than exact; it is a science of tendencies. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that government intervention is the best way to achieve equity.
items.answer: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets distribute according to purchasing power, not need; taxes and transfers can redistribute effectively; governments can provide merit goods to all. Arguments against: intervention can reduce incentives and efficiency; government failure: poorly targeted policies; NGOs, communities and firms (CSR) also improve equity. Judgement: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples.
